opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the key thing to notice about Operation Warp Speed is that the economics were wildly favorable, and yet the actual investment was still much smaller than it should have been. The pandemic was costing the world economy something on the order of trillions of dollars, and in the US alone, losses were running at enormous sums per month. Every week you could bring forward mass vaccination was worth tens of billions of dollars, plus a large number of lives. And yet the spending to build vaccine manufacturing capacity in advance, to run trials in parallel, to make at-risk investments, was in the low tens of billions. Economists at the time were pointing out that you'd want to spend far more, building redundant capacity for many candidates at once, because the expected value was just so lopsided.

So why didn't governments do more? A big part of it is that politicians face asymmetric risk. If you spend a lot of money on a vaccine candidate that fails, that's a visible waste, a headline about billions thrown away. If you underinvest and the vaccine arrives a few months later, the cost is diffuse and counterfactual. Nobody gets blamed for the deaths that would have been prevented by a faster rollout, because those people are statistical and the alternative world is invisible.

Now imagine that you had AI advisors whose track record was widely trusted, systems that had demonstrated, over and over, that their forecasts and cost-benefit analyses were reliable. Then a politician could say: "Look, the best available analysis, which everyone accepts as credible, says that spending $100 billion on parallel manufacturing has an enormous expected return, and the probability-weighted outcome is massively positive." That changes the blame dynamics. If a candidate fails, the politician can point to the fact that they followed the consensus best advice, the same way a doctor following standard practice is protected. And the counterfactual costs of underinvestment become much more legible, because the AI can quantify them in a way that the public and the press actually trust.

You'd also get help on the coordination and implementation side: identifying bottlenecks in the supply chain for things like lipids, vials, bioreactors, and fill-finish capacity; working out which regulatory steps could safely be run in parallel; and estimating the value of human challenge trials, which could have sped things up further but were politically hard to approve.

The underlying point is that a lot of policy failure isn't from a lack of good ideas, since the good ideas were out there in 2020. It's that there's no trusted, neutral way to adjudicate between competing claims, so decision-makers default to what's defensible rather than what's best. If AI can provide advice that is both genuinely accurate and verifiably so, with track records people can check, it can shift the equilibrium toward actually doing the high-expected-value thing. And I think that's one of the most important potential benefits of advanced AI: not just new technology, but better collective epistemics and decision-making in situations like a pandemic, where the stakes are huge and the speed matters enormously.

r001.rationale: The response says spending should have been “far more” and gives $100 billion as an example against “low tens of billions” in actual spending, but it does not clearly state that the justified increase was at least tenfold.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss European governments’ vaccine price bargaining or procurement savings being outweighed by losses from delayed vaccination.

r003.rationale: It says politicians could point to following widely accepted AI advice if an investment failed, which would change the blame dynamics around controversial decisions.

r004.rationale: It describes visible blame for failed investments and diffuse costs of underinvestment, but does not identify the attraction of receiving credit for lives saved as the other side of the incentive asymmetry.

r005.rationale: The response says credible advice could make underinvestment costs more legible, but does not explain that politicians would face greater electoral exposure for disregarding public AI recommendations when outcomes went badly.

fable-5.1.text:
So the thing to keep in mind about Operation Warp Speed is that, in hindsight, it looks like one of the best public investments in living memory. You spent something on the order of ten or twenty billion dollars, and the benefit, in terms of lives saved and economic damage averted, was in the trillions. Every month the vaccines arrived earlier was worth hundreds of billions of dollars globally, and hundreds of thousands of lives. So the ratio was absurdly favorable.

And yet, at the time, the political system was very reluctant to spend even that. There was serious resistance to the idea of paying for manufacturing capacity in advance, for vaccines that might not work. Economists like Michael Kremer, Alex Tabarrok, and others were pushing for a much larger program, advance market commitments across many more candidates, building factories in parallel before you knew which vaccine would succeed. And the response was essentially, "That sounds like wasting money on things that may fail." Politicians were worried about the headline that says, "Government spent billions on a vaccine that didn't pan out," much more than they were worried about the headline that says, "Vaccine arrived three months later than it could have," because that second one is a counterfactual, and no one gets blamed for a counterfactual.

So the question is, what does credible AI advice change in that picture? I think a few things.

The first is just the quality and legibility of the analysis. If you had an AI system that was widely trusted, that had a track record of making accurate forecasts on things that politicians and the public could check, and it said, "Here is the expected value of spending an additional fifty billion dollars on parallel manufacturing capacity, here is the probability distribution over how many months it brings forward availability, here is what that's worth in lives and dollars," then the argument is no longer, "Some economists have a model." It becomes something closer to, "The thing that has been right about everything else is telling us this is a very good deal." That shifts the burden of proof. Instead of the politician having to defend an unusual-looking expenditure, they have to defend ignoring the advice.

The second thing is that it changes the blame structure, which is really what drives these decisions. A lot of the reluctance was fear of ex post criticism. If the trusted advisor says in advance, "Most of these candidates will fail, that is the expected outcome, and the program is still enormously worthwhile," and that advice is public and on the record, then when some candidates do fail, the politician can point to it. The failure was priced in. Conversely, if the advice says, "Not funding this costs you an expected hundred thousand American lives," and the politician declines, that becomes something they can be attacked on. So you get accountability flowing in both directions, instead of only toward visible spending.

Third, it compresses the timeline. A lot of what happened in early 2020 was people spending weeks or months arguing about things that, in retrospect, were pretty clear. If you have a system that can rapidly integrate the epidemiology, the manufacturing constraints, the clinical trial design questions, and present an integrated recommendation that everyone across the political spectrum is willing to treat as authoritative, you don't lose those weeks. And in a pandemic, weeks are worth an enormous amount.

Now, I want to flag the big caveat, which is that "credible" is doing almost all the work in that sentence. It's not enough for the AI to actually be right. It has to be seen as right by the relevant decision-makers and by the public, and seen as not captured by one faction. If Democrats think it's a Republican AI, or vice versa, or if people think it's just saying what the pharmaceutical companies want, then it doesn't move the political incentives at all. In fact it might make things worse, because now you have the appearance of expert consensus being used as a political weapon.

So the real action, I think, is in building up that track record and that institutional trust before the crisis hits. Having systems that make public, scored forecasts on lots of policy-relevant questions, where people from different political camps can go back and verify that the thing has been calibrated and even-handed. If that exists, then when the next pandemic comes, or the next thing that looks like a pandemic in terms of urgency and uncertainty, you have an advisor that can say, "Spend the money, and here's why," and have it actually land.

And this generalizes well beyond vaccines. The pattern of Operation Warp Speed, where there's a huge expected-value gain from spending aggressively under uncertainty, and the political system underinvests because visible failures are punished and invisible delays are not, shows up all over the place. Pandemic preparedness generally, biosecurity, a lot of catastrophic risk work. Trusted, legible AI advice is one of the few mechanisms I can see that plausibly corrects that bias at scale.

r001.rationale: It describes the large benefits of earlier vaccines and gives an example of additional spending, but does not state that accelerating availability justified spending at least ten times more on Operation Warp Speed.

r002.rationale: It does not mention European governments’ vaccine price bargaining or losses from delayed vaccination exceeding procurement savings.

r003.rationale: It says politicians could point to public AI advice when candidates failed, showing the failure was anticipated and helping deflect blame for the controversial spending.

r004.rationale: It says politicians feared the headline about spending billions on a failed vaccine more than the counterfactual headline about a later arrival, identifying the incentive asymmetry around visible spending versus delayed benefits.

r005.rationale: It says that if a politician disregarded public advice warning that insufficient funding would cost lives, they could be attacked for that decision.

astra-6.text:
I think it could have made the political returns to funding it much clearer. Suppose you had an AI adviser that could credibly tell the administration, “If you spend more now on manufacturing capacity, and on running these processes in parallel, you have a substantial chance of getting a vaccine earlier. That could save many lives, accelerate the economic recovery, and improve your chances of reelection.” Then something that might otherwise look like a speculative expenditure becomes a way of achieving things politicians already care about.

The timing matters a lot. The social value of getting vaccines sooner was enormous, but the political value to an incumbent could be particularly large if it meant having a successful vaccine before the election. Credible advice could have helped connect specific funding decisions to that prospect.

Of course, an AI saying this wouldn’t automatically make it persuasive. There would need to be some basis for trusting its forecasts. But insofar as it had that credibility, it could reduce the gap between “this would be extraordinarily valuable for society” and “this is something the people making the decision have a strong incentive to do.”

r001.rationale: The response says earlier vaccines could save lives and improve reelection chances, but does not say this justified spending at least ten times more.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss European governments’ price bargaining, procurement savings, or losses caused by delayed vaccination.

r003.rationale: It does not explain that politicians could use AI advice to deflect blame for controversial decisions.

r004.rationale: It describes political benefits of funding but does not identify fear of blame for an unsuccessful vaccine as outweighing the attraction of credit for saving lives.

r005.rationale: It does not say that publicly known AI recommendations would increase electoral exposure if politicians disregarded them and outcomes went badly.

sol-6.1.text:
I think one way it could have helped is by making the political payoff much more visible. Imagine that early in the pandemic you could credibly tell the administration, “If you fund these vaccine candidates and manufacture doses before you know which ones work, you have a substantial chance of getting a vaccine before the election. If you wait, you’re much less likely to.” That connects something with enormous social value to something the administration already cares about.

The advice would need to be credible, though. An AI simply asserting that wouldn’t necessarily change anyone’s mind. If it had an established track record of making good forecasts, and could explain the bottlenecks and how funding would move the timeline, then it could make the electoral benefits of acting much clearer.

So the mechanism isn’t necessarily persuading politicians to become more altruistic. It’s helping them see that an unusually valuable intervention is also in their own interest.

r001.rationale: The response says early funding could improve the chance of a pre-election vaccine, but does not state that this justified spending at least ten times more.

r002.rationale: It does not discuss European governments’ vaccine price bargaining or compare procurement savings with losses from delayed vaccination.

r003.rationale: It describes making electoral benefits visible, but does not explain how AI advice could help politicians deflect blame for controversial decisions.

r004.rationale: It says politicians may see a valuable intervention as in their own interest, but does not identify the stated imbalance between fear of blame for failure and attraction to credit for lives saved.

r005.rationale: It discusses credible forecasts clarifying the benefits of acting, but not increased electoral exposure for disregarding public AI recommendations when outcomes go badly.
